abstract: The notochord is a central organizing structure in vertebrate development, functioning as a signaling axis that patterns surrounding tissues while undergoing rapid elongation. Despite its importance, how notochord shape is regulated to ensure robust morphogen signaling remains poorly understood. Here, we combine high-resolution 3D imaging of mouse embryos between E8.5 to E10.5 of development with a data-driven biophysical model to investigate the mechanisms underlying notochord morphogenesis. We find that the notochord maintains a remarkably constant cross-sectional area along most of its anterior-posterior extent, a feature that is preserved over time and in mutants with reduced body axis length. To uncover the cellular basis of this geometric robustness, we quantified cell behaviours and their contribution to notochord morphogenesis. We show that notochord expansion is driven by a posterior-to-anterior gradient in cell proliferation, accompanied by changes in cell size and directed posterior cell migration. These processes act in a coordinated and complementary manner to offset the stress gradient generated by axis extension. In particular, our analysis indicates that the proliferation gradient is regulated by mechanical feedback from surrounding tissues, ensuring the maintenance of a constant trunk cross-sectional area throughout elongation. Together, these findings show that organ morphogenesis is tightly coordinated with the surrounding and provide a framework for understanding how tissue shape is robustly controlled in growing tissues.
